title: My True Child in Our Common Faith
subtitle: Titus 1:1–4
description: Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, greets Titus, his true child in the common faith, under the hope promised before time began by the God who cannot lie.
paragraphs: The shortest of Paul's letters to a coworker opens by stating his commission before it greets a single person. Paul calls himself “a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ,” a pairing he uses in no other greeting, and he gives the commission its purpose at once: “for the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness.” The apostle's work and the truth belong together in his telling, measured by whether the truth produces godliness in the people who hear it.

Under everything stands a hope with a timestamp older than time. The commission runs “in the hope of eternal life,” and the hope rests on a promise made by a God defined by what he cannot do: “which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began.” The promise waited through ages, and then, Paul says, “In His own time He has made His word evident in the proclamation entrusted to me by the command of God our Savior.”

Only then does the letter turn to its reader. “To Titus, my true child in our common faith,” Paul writes, using the same fatherly language he used to Timothy, and the greeting follows: “Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.” Grace and peace only, where his greetings to Timothy added mercy; the letter states the difference and builds nothing on it.

What follows this greeting is a working letter of under a thousand words: elders to appoint on an island full of talkers, households to teach, and a winter plan at Nicopolis. It begins, as Paul's letters do, with who he is, whose Titus is, and the hope that was promised before time began.

title: Set in Order What Was Unfinished
subtitle: Titus 1:5–9
description: Titus is left in Crete to set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town: blameless men, God's stewards, holding firmly to the faithful word.
paragraphs: Crete was left mid-job, and Titus was the man left holding it. “The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you.” Churches existed across the island; leadership did not, and finishing that work was Titus's assignment.

Picture the state of things. The gospel had reached town after town across the island, people had believed and gathered, and then the planting work had moved on with its work unfinished: no appointed leadership, no settled order, and, as the next episode shows, talkers already filling the vacuum. Titus is not sent to found the work but to finish it, and the appointing is deliberately local. Elders in every town, plural men in each place, drawn from the congregations themselves rather than imported. And the first word of the standard, blameless, does not mean a man who has never failed. It means a man against whom no charge sticks, whose life gives an accuser nothing to hold.

The standard for the men he appoints starts at home. “An elder must be blameless, the husband of but one wife, having children who are believers” and who are “not open to accusation of indiscretion or insubordination.” A man's household is the first evidence of whether he can be trusted with God's.

Then the letter shifts its word from elder to overseer and raises the same standard again. “As God’s steward, an overseer must be above reproach,” and the failures are named first: “not self-willed, not quick-tempered, not given to drunkenness, not violent, not greedy for money.” Against them stands the positive shape: he must “be hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined.”

The word steward carries weight of its own. A steward managed a household and property that belonged to someone else, and answered to the owner for all of it. Paul has already said the elder's own household is the first evidence; now the church is named as God's household, with the overseer answerable for a household that is not his. The list stands beside the overseer list Paul gave Timothy, near enough in shape to be recognized and different enough in wording to be its own letter's own standard, and neither list is edited by the other.

The last requirement is about the word itself. “He must hold firmly to the faithful word as it was taught, so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it.” Crete's problem, as the next passage shows, was talkers. The elder Titus appoints has to be able to answer them, and a man who will not hold the word himself cannot.

title: Silence the Empty Talkers
subtitle: Titus 1:10–16
description: Rebellious empty talkers undermine entire households for gain; a Cretan prophet's own verdict is quoted, and those who profess to know God are measured by their actions.
paragraphs: The reason elders must be able to refute is standing in the same room. “For many are rebellious and full of empty talk and deception, especially those of the circumcision,” Paul writes, and his instruction is blunt: they “must be silenced.” The damage is domestic, not abstract: “For the sake of dishonorable gain, they undermine entire households and teach things they should not.”

Then Paul quotes a Cretan against the Cretans. “As one of their own prophets has said,” he writes, and the saying stands as its own sentence: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.” Tradition names the prophet as Epimenides, a Cretan poet from centuries earlier, and Paul does not soften the verdict his witness gave: “This testimony is true.” The purpose is restoration, not contempt: “rebuke them sternly, so that they will be sound in the faith” and “pay no attention to Jewish myths or to the commands of men who have rejected the truth.”

Their identity is sketched in two strokes. Especially those of the circumcision marks them as teachers from a Jewish background, and the myths and commandments they push are the wares the letter keeps naming: Jewish myths, and commands issued by men who have themselves rejected the truth. The paradox is the point. Men busy commanding others about purity stand exposed as defiled in mind and conscience, and their commands carry no authority because their own lives have already answered them.

Notice where the talkers do their work. Households were the units of the ancient world: families, servants, and dependents who believed and lived together under one roof, which is why an error that captured a household captured a whole small community at once. And the gain named as their motive explains the method: teaching shaped to please paying hearers spreads faster than teaching that corrects them. That is why the silencing is not optional courtesy. It is the protection of homes.

The principle underneath is about what a person has become inside. “To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure.” Indeed, “both their minds and their consciences are defiled.” And the talkers' own religion is measured by their conduct: “They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him.” The letter's verdict on that profession is severe: “They are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed.”

title: Teach What Fits Sound Doctrine
subtitle: Titus 2:1–10
description: Speak what fits sound doctrine: older men and women, young women trained at home, younger men, Titus himself as the example, and slaves adorning the teaching.
paragraphs: Against the empty talkers, Titus gets a different assignment: “speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine.” What follows is doctrine taught by household, group by group. “Older men are to be temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance.” Older women, likewise, are to be “not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good.”

Their teaching post is the young women of the church: they are to “train the young women to love their husbands and children,” “to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands.” The reason given is the reputation of the message itself, “so that the word of God will not be discredited.”

One feature of the design deserves a plain look: the teaching travels hand to hand. Titus teaches, the older women train the younger, and the doctrine moves through the household's own relationships instead of arriving only from a public platform. And the young women's first lesson is an affection, to love their husbands and children, treated here as something that can be trained and practiced rather than simply felt, with the management of the household named as real responsibility in the home's daily economy.

The younger men get one charge, “to be self-controlled,” and Titus himself gets the method: “show yourself to be an example by doing good works,” with teaching marked by integrity, dignity, and “wholesome speech that is above reproach.” The aim looks outward again: “so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us.”

The pattern across the groups is worth seeing plainly. Sound doctrine in this chapter is never measured by how it sounds in a gathering. It is measured group by group, in tempers kept, tongues governed, homes managed, and work done honestly when no one with power is watching. And the teacher stands inside his own teaching: where the talkers of the first chapter professed to know God and denied him by their actions, Titus is ordered to be the opposite exhibit, a man whose deeds and whose doctrine say the same thing.

Last come the slaves in those households, who have the least standing of anyone addressed. “Slaves are to submit to their own masters in everything,” “not stealing from them, but showing all good faith,” and the reason given them is the highest in the chapter: “so that in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior.” Even the people with no public voice are told their conduct decorates the doctrine.

title: The Grace of God Has Appeared
subtitle: Titus 2:11–15
description: The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone, instructing godly lives in the present age while awaiting the blessed hope and glorious appearance.
paragraphs: Underneath all the household instruction stands one event. “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone.” Grace in this letter is not only pardon; it is a teacher. “It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age.”

And it teaches its students to watch. The godly life is lived “as we await the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,” in the letter's exact words for the one who is coming.

The scope is stated without a fence around it: salvation brought to everyone, in an island letter written to small household churches surrounded by neighbors who had not believed. And the age the students live in is named the present age, a phrase that only makes sense against another age coming, which is exactly what the watching is for. Grace's curriculum, in other words, is aimed at people who live between an appearing that has happened and an appearing that has not.

The ground of it all is a gift given by the one who comes. “He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness” and “to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds.” Redeemed from lawlessness and owned for good deeds: the two halves of the sentence are the whole letter in miniature, and the zeal Paul wants is zeal aimed at deeds, not arguments.

One word stitches this letter together, and it appears here at its center: appeared. Grace has appeared. The appearing of God's kindness will open the next chapter's great passage, and the glorious appearing of Christ is what the church awaits between them. Salvation in this letter is something that shows up in the world and can be pointed to, first in grace, then in kindness, and at the end in glory. And the zeal is redirected on purpose: Crete's talkers burn with zeal for arguments and myths, while the people grace creates burn with zeal for good deeds done to actual neighbors.

So the charge to Titus closes the movement. “Speak these things as you encourage and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.” The young delegate is not to apologize for the message. Grace appeared, grace instructs, grace is coming again, and Titus is to say so with the authority the letter itself carries.

title: He Saved Us, Not by Our Deeds
subtitle: Titus 3:1–8
description: Be peaceable and gentle to everyone, remembering what we once were; God saved us not by our righteous deeds but by his mercy, through the washing of new birth.
paragraphs: The last chapter opens by turning the believers outward, toward the society around them. “Remind the believers to submit to rulers and authorities, to be obedient and ready for every good work,” Paul writes, “to malign no one, and to be peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone.”

The order is given without qualifications about which rulers or how deserving they are, in a province governed by Rome and an island famous in the letter itself for disorder. The church's outward posture is set in advance: obedient, ready for good work, refusing slander, gentle with everyone. It completes the household picture of the chapter before it. Chapter two ordered the believers' life at home; this chapter opens the front door.

The reason is a remembered past, and Paul includes himself in it. “For at one time we too were foolish, disobedient, misled, and enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures,” “living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another.” Gentleness toward outsiders is built on honesty about what the believers used to be.

Then the letter's second great appearing answers the first. “But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared,” everything changed, and the ground of it is stated with care: “He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.” The Spirit in that washing is no trickle: “This is the Spirit He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior,” “so that, having been justified by His grace, we would become heirs with the hope of eternal life.”

The passage also closes the letter's own frame. The greeting promised eternal life from the God who cannot lie, promised before time began; here the saved are named heirs with that same hope, the promise arriving at its people. And the washing language sits in the letter without apology or explanation, the renewal of the Holy Spirit named as the means and mercy named as the ground. Readers have long described that washing differently among themselves; the letter itself simply states it and moves on to what it produces.

Over the whole passage Paul sets his seal: “This saying is trustworthy.” And the practical end of it is the letter's drumbeat one more time: he wants these things emphasized “so that those who have believed God will take care to devote themselves to good deeds.” Then the summary: “These things are excellent and profitable for the people.” Saved by mercy, not deeds, and therefore devoted to deeds; the letter holds both without blinking.

title: Devote Yourselves to Good Works
subtitle: Titus 3:9–15
description: Avoid foolish controversies, reject the divisive after two warnings, equip Zenas and Apollos, come to Nicopolis, and devote yourselves to good works. Grace be with all of you.
paragraphs: The letter closes by clearing the ground around its own message. “But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law, because these things are pointless and worthless.” And the man who feeds on division gets a procedure with an end: “Reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition,” “knowing that such a man is corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned.”

Even the discipline has patience built into it. A divisive man is not cut off at the first offense or the second warning; he is admonished once, then again, and only then rejected, and the letter's reason is diagnostic rather than angry: after two warnings refused, the man has shown his own state, corrupt and self-condemned, condemning himself by the refusals. The procedure is slow enough to be fair and firm enough to end.

Then the travel plans, as practical as everything else in the letter. “As soon as I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis, because I have decided to winter there.” Titus is not being abandoned in Crete; he is being relieved, and the handoff is planned. Two more travelers are Titus's responsibility before he leaves: “Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need.”

The names are the letter in miniature. Artemas appears nowhere else in Paul's letters and is introduced without a word of explanation, because Titus knew him. Zenas carries his trade in his title, a lawyer traveling in the apostolic circle. Apollos, the teacher known from Corinth's story, is on the road again. The church's job toward all three is unglamorous and concrete: supplies, money, and speed on their way, the same practical care the letter has been teaching from its first chapter.

The last instruction returns to the drumbeat, widened now to everyone. “And our people must also learn to devote themselves to good works in order to meet the pressing needs of others, so that they will not be unfruitful.” Good works in this letter are not decoration; they are how pressing needs get met.

The greetings carry the same warmth as the greeting that opened the letter. “All who are with me send you greetings. Greet those who love us in the faith.” And over a hard assignment on a hard island, the final word is the one the letter kept circling: “Grace be with all of you.”
